div.p: Modern control systems, including robotics, drones, and autonomous vehicles, are increasingly incorporating intelligent controllers such as deep neural networks (DNNs) supported by heterogeneous processors. However, unlike conventional control algorithms on homogeneous platforms, the design and runtime execution of intelligent control tasks on heterogeneous computing platforms pose more rigorous demands and substantial challenges. These challenges encompass not only inherent conflicts between algorithm complexity and accuracy but also the couplings and trade-offs among run-time execution latency, end-to-end system performance, and reliability with timing constraints. To address these challenges, this paper introduces an end-to-end capability and scheduling co-design approach to efficiently design intelligent control tasks on heterogeneous computing architectures. We first introduce a novel and general control capability function, which bridges the control performance with the complexity of the intelligent controller, computation latency, and the properties of the physical plants. Subsequently, we formulate a comprehensive optimization problem to properly design algorithm capability and assign limited heterogeneous computational resources from offline heterogeneous resource allocation to run-time execution. Finally, we present a case study on the intelligent control of autonomous quadcopters (with the hardware-in-the-loop simulator built on Microsoft AirSim), and the extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the capability and scheduling co-design in terms of overall system performance compared with state-of-the-art design approaches.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Modern control systems, such as robotics, drones, and autonomous vehicles, are embracing artificial intelligencebased intelligent control, which means the feedback control laws that generate actuation commands based on run-time physical states are data-driven/machine learning (ML)-based approaches, to serve complex and diverse control task and performance requirements. For example, deep neural networks (DNNs) have made significant strides in feedback control in recent years by leveraging the combined advantages of ML for scalability and analytical traceability [1]- [3]. Meanwhile, to accommodate the demands of executing ML-based algorithms and accelerating computations, the landscape of computing platforms is evolving towards heterogeneous computing architecture, which integrates diverse computing resources such as CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs [4], [5]. By incorporating accelerators, such as GPUs, alongside traditional CPUs, intelligent Fig. 1: Intelligent controller on heterogeneous computing with capability and runtime scheduling co-design. control strategies can be accelerated, which is particularly crucial in intelligent feedback control scenarios with strict timing constraints. However, the state-of-the-art intelligent control for autonomous machines is growing increasingly complex, leading to substantial challenges in design efforts, run-time latency, and reliability [6], [7].

Mainstream ML tasks are generally assessed based on measures of accuracy, which are closely related to the complexity and scale of the algorithm [8], [9]. However, for intelligent controllers, the primary design objective is to enhance control performance, such as minimizing physical state errors from reference values or reducing settling time. A gap emerges between control performance in real systems and ML algorithm accuracy, as control performance is influenced not only by the precision of the intelligent controller in deriving optimal control strategies but also by the characteristics of the physical plants involved. Additionally, the disparity between computation latency and the eventual intelligent control performance exacerbates this gap due to the real-time actuation nature of intelligent controllers. Furthermore, when multiple intelligent control tasks are executed concurrently on the same computational platform to meet real-time requirements, the complexities of computation-intensive algorithms must be restricted and properly balanced due to limited computational resources. Real-time performance is also notably affected by the execution method employed for these intelligent control tasks. Unlike conventional homogeneous processors, the interleaved execution pattern across heterogeneous processors intensifies the dependencies and competition among parallel tasks, leading to unpredictable control performance [10].

In this study, we propose general and comprehensive control capability tailored for real-time intelligent control systems. Instead of optimizing the common accuracy metrics of ML tasks, the control capability of an intelligent controller describes how control performance is affected by the scale/complexity of the controller. Since control performance is coupled with the model scale/complexity of the intelligent controller and its worst-case response time, as well as the physical dynamics, control capability should be presented as a functional relationship with the key configuration variable of controller scale/complexity. Notably, the capability of the intelligent controller should depend on the properties of the physical plants and the resource limitation. A plant with a short time constant (more time-sensitive) may rely on a lightweight controller to make sure quick generation of the control commands instead of pursuing extreme ML model accuracy. However, the lightweight controller may result in unnecessary control performance loss for a plant that has a long time constant (less time-sensitive). In addition, limited computation resources and real-time scheduling strategy should be dynamically assigned to multiple control intelligent controllers in order to optimize the control performance of all physical plants. Resource allocation and scheduling strategy should bidirectionally interact with the capability of controllers according to the properties of the physical plants.

Therefore, we introduce an innovative end-to-end approach for co-designing the capability and scheduling of intelligent controllers, as shown in Fig. 1. Our methodology begins by proposing and constructing control capability functions to address the complexity and coupling inherent in intelligent controllers, computational execution, physical plant properties, and actual control performance. Leveraging the capability function, we develop a comprehensive framework to determine algorithmic capabilities and allocate limited heterogeneous computational resources. This process spans both offline heterogeneous resource allocation and real-time execution stages. Furthermore, as a case study to evaluate the capability and scheduling co-design for intelligent real-time control systems, we build a hardware-in-the-loop simulator that integrates real heterogeneous computing platforms and the Microsoft AirSim simulator for autonomous quadcopters. The contributions are four-fold.

‚ The definition and characterization of the control capability function are introduced, delineating the interrelations among control performance, algorithmic complexity, latency, and physical plant properties. ‚ A comprehensive model of the intelligent controller is developed, encompassing both intelligent control algorithms and computation task execution models on heterogeneous platforms. This integrated model seamlessly merges controller design with heterogeneous resource scheduling. ‚ A co-design of capability and scheduling is established, aiming to determine optimal capability, resource allocation, and real-time scheduling strategies. This approach furnishes an end-to-end solution tailored for ML-based intelligent controllers. ‚ A hardware-in-the-loop simulator is built, integrating real heterogeneous computing platforms for executing intel-ligent control tasks and AirSim for simulating physical plants. The case study on autonomous drones demonstrates the advantages of the proposed approaches. The remainder of the article is organized as follows. Sec. III presents the intelligent control architecture and the definition and derivation of the control capability function. Sec. IV introduces the modeling of the intelligent controllers from the perspective of algorithm and heterogeneous resource mapping. Sec. V presents the co-design of the capability and scheduling for ML-based intelligent controllers. Sec. VI describes the hardware-in-the-loop simulator developments and performance evaluation for intelligent quadcopter control. Sec. II and Sec. VII review related works and conclude this paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Analytical optimal controllers, such as linear quadratic regulator (LQR) and model predictive control (MPC), can generate the optimal control policy for complex systems. However, their computational complexity is too high to meet the realtime requirements under high control frequency, especially for complicated nonlinear systems [11], [12]. To overcome the limitation of analytical approaches, data-driven techniques provide new tools for intelligent control. Intelligence technologies, such as DNNs, have led to revolutionary changes in the control of robotics [13], [14], multi-agent systems [15]- [17], and industrial automation [18]- [20] in recent years. Chen et al. [1] use NNs to approximate the optimal control laws. Klaučo et al. [2] propose to apply ML to accelerate primal active set methods used to solve quadratic programming (QP)based MPC problems. However, all the above works assume that the computation platform of intelligent control policies is a black box and overlooks the dynamics and potential benefits in the runtime execution.

The impacts of computation on the performance of control systems with analytical controllers have been explored by analytical methods, where control performance is modeled as functions of latency, rate, etc. Maggio et al. [21] analyze the stability of control systems with a controller that can sporadically miss deadlines. Vreman et al. [22] extend the research of control systems with bursts of deadline misses and explore the design of controllers. Cervin et al. [23] adapt the period of control tasks to minimize the overall control performance on a single-CPU platform. Pazzaglia et al. [24] consider the linear quadratic regulators subject to weaklyhard constraints. Saifullah et al. [25] determine sampling rates to optimize control performance in terms of linear quadratic metrics. However, analytical control performance metrics over various computation configurations cannot be derived for the intelligent control systems, since the data-driven controllers cannot be modeled analytically, let alone the targeted plants, and control tasks of intelligent controllers are usually complex and difficult. Moreover, while it has been demonstrated that the performance of the ML-based algorithm is closely related to the complexity/scale of the algorithm, in the perspective of model accuracy [8], [9], [26], [27], for intelligent controllers, improving the control performance are the main design goals. However, a gap arises between the closed-loop control performance and the ML inference complexity and accuracy, which has not been addressed yet. This work proposes the control capability function to bridge this gap.

It has been stated that the runtime task scheduling strategies affect control performances. For example, Dai et al. [28] adapt the period of control tasks at runtime, considering the task set with one control task and multiple non-control tasks. Wu et al. [29] propose composite resource scheduling in realtime networked control systems with a strict execution order, which guarantees the resource utilization constraints. Bini et al. [30], [31] explore sensitivity analysis and delay-aware modeling to adapt control rates/periods in control-scheduling co-design, significantly reducing the implementation-induced performance degradation, especially for large control tasksets and delay-sensitive plants. However, the above real-time control designs focus on tasks running on single processors or multiple homogeneous processors or wireless network scheduling, which cannot support computationally expensive intelligent control, especially on today's heterogeneous computing platforms.

Working with the general DNN workload on heterogeneous platforms, Xiang et al. [32] propose DART, which allocates heterogeneous resources to DNNs on the layer level with response time analysis and optimizes worst-case execution time. Kang et al. [33] introduce quantization and runtime layer migration to reduce inference time. Ling et al. [34] adopt operator fusion to optimize the execution time of DNNs. The deadline miss rate of real-time tasks is reduced through blocklevel optimization for parallel DNNs. Previous studies have not adequately addressed the complexity and scale of intelligent algorithms for control systems, encountering challenges in creating a general, end-to-end approach for facilitating intelligent control tasks on modern heterogeneous architectures. To address these issues, we introduce a capability and scheduling co-design approach that optimizes both algorithm capabilities and limited heterogeneous computational resources.

div.head: III. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE WITH CONTROL CAPABILITY
div.p: In intelligent control systems, the states of physical plants-such as the position and velocity of drones or the joint position of robotic arms-are monitored and regulated by intelligent controllers, which are executed as computational tasks on heterogeneous computing platforms. These controllers interface with the sensors and actuators of the physical plants through fast and reliable communication networks. However, accommodating intelligent controllers on heterogeneous computation platforms presents open challenges for control systems with stringent requirements, including (1) achieving optimal control performance, the central objective of any control system, (2) determining proper capability for the intelligent controller, and (3) maintaining reliable real-time performance, essential and prerequisite for the smooth and timely execution of intelligent controllers under limited heterogeneous computational resources. This section first provides an overview of the intelligent control architecture and then presents the definition and derivation of the capability of an intelligent controller.

div.head: A. Intelligent Control over Heterogeneous Platforms
div.p: As illustrated in Fig. 2, the proposed intelligent controller utilizes a comprehensive end-to-end architecture that bridges controller design and control task execution across multiple control loops on heterogeneous computational platforms. From the controller design perspective, we exploit the intertwined relationships among control performance, and controller complexity * , and real-time performance at runtime. We propose a novel function, control capability, to describe and derive them. From the perspective of task execution, the heterogeneous computation platform concurrently executes real-time intelligent control policies (i.e., DNN tasks) for multiple physical plants, with their own sampling/control periods. The system benefits from both high-granularity resource allocation and real-time scheduling of limited heterogeneous computational resources, ensuring reliable and efficient execution and final control performance. Resource allocation and realtime scheduling are two modules that collaboratively improve control performance. Resource allocation is determined offline, assigning heterogeneous computation resources at layered granularity and mapping the layered model of DNNs to segmented task model based on the assignments. Real-time scheduling includes offline and online stages. In the offline stage, the WCRT and schedulability analysis are derived. In the online stage, tasks are scheduled based on priorities.

The proposed SCENIC begins by establishing the control capability function through data-driven methodologies, while concurrently analyzing the interconnected cyber and physical properties within each control loop. During the runtime stage, control tasks are scheduled based on assigned task priorities derived from the optimization problem. This prioritization informs the generation of actuation commands, which are based on sensor measurements, facilitating the closure of the control loops.

div.head: REMARK. 1:
div.p: In this work, since we mainly focus on heterogeneous computation resource scheduling and control capability co-design, we assume the network is reliable [36]- [38]. In reality, network reliability directly impacts on control performance, which is not the focus of this work. Interested readers are referred to [39], [40] for run-time network reconfigurations and [41], [42] for local and edge controller co-designs to optimize control performance. In our future work, we will take network reliability and scheduling into consideration in order to explore a more comprehensive heterogeneous scheduling design of both heterogeneous computation and communication platforms as integrity, tailored for intelligent control systems.

2) Control Task Modeling: The control policy for each loop is regarded as the periodic control task, τ i , i P t1, 2, 3, ..., N u, with a period of T i . The deadlines D i of control tasks are equal to their periods, i.e., D i " T i . Control tasks τ i share the heterogeneous cores, i.e., CPU, GPUs, etc. We target the most fundamental case, which has multiple CPU cores and accelerator cores, such as GPU SMs or FPGA IP cores [32]. Any heterogeneous system can be regarded as an extension of this fundamental case. The CPU cores apply real-time scheduling by the operating system (OS) and support the preemption, but each accelerator core is generally not preemptive [34], [43].

One of the classic task models on heterogeneous architecture is the self-suspending segmented task model [44], [45], which can be expressed as a 3-tuple, c i of each DNN intelligent controller, the physical dynamics parameters θ i in f i and g i , and the end-to-end worst-case response time R i of the control tasks. The response time R i is measured from the moment the physical states x i pkq are recorded to the moment the control commands u i pkq are actuated on the physical plants. For instance, at time t " kT i , the physical state x i pkq is measured. It takes R i to transmit x i pkq to the intelligent controller, execute the control task to derive control commands u i pkq, and transmit u i pkq to the actuator of the physical plant i. At time t " kT i `Ri , u i pkq is actuated. Furthermore, the control performance is affected by the environmental conditions ϵ i that the physical plants are working at, which equips the control performance function with environment-aware features.

div.head: IV. MODELING OF INTELLIGENT CONTROLLER A. Intelligent Control Algorithm
div.p: As we know, solving the underlying optimization problems in analytical controllers for complex physical plant dynamics, which are usually high-dimensional and nonlinear, could be computationally expensive and intractable [35], [46]. We use analytical (MPC) and intelligent (DNN) controllers for quadcopters as illustrative examples. The details of the controller designs and control task execution setups are presented in Section IV-C. As shown in Table II, the profiled worst-case execution time (PWCET) of MPC is up to 131.59 ms, which is significantly longer compared to DNN. Additionally, the complexity and capability of DNN can be precisely designed and executed as computational tasks accelerated by the heterogeneous platform.

The intelligent controller is designed with DNN models g i,ci p¨q with different complexity c i for the physical plant i to learn the analytical optimal controller, which can be any analytical optimal control policy, such as LQR, MPC, path planning, etc. The intelligent controller g i,ci p¨q is trained by labeled data generated offline. The detailed process of developing the intelligent controllers with different complexities are presented in the online document [47]. Afterward, the trained models with different c i are selected by the capability and scheduling co-design problem, which is described in Sec. V, and deployed onto the heterogeneous computation platform. The intelligent controller generates the control commands u i pkq based on current states at each control period at runtime.

At the same time, realtime scheduling performance is analyzed at the segment level to reduce scheduling and analysis complexity. div.head: C. Intelligent Controller for Autonomous Quadcopters
div.p: We present the intelligent controller for an autonomous quadcopter control system as a case study, from both perspectives of algorithm and task execution. This intelligent controller is also evaluated with the hardware-in-the-loop simulator that integrates heterogeneous computing platforms and AirSim (see Sec. VI for the detailed experimental settings).

Data Collection: The processes of path planning and MPC are repeated several times under different initial inputs with 10 random initial plant states and 150 environment conditions, to generate training data. The corresponding input and output vectors are recorded over 5 s, which is the average interval of time when the quadcopter begins to receive control commands until it reaches the gate. And the control/sampling period is T i " 0.05 s. Thus 150 ¨10 ¨100 " 150, 000 pairs of labeled data are collected to train intelligent controllers.

Model Training: In this work, we train fully-connected (FC) feedforward DNNs with different c i , i.e., different sizes of L i and o i,j . Note the activation functions are also regarded as layers, which depend on o i,j of the preceding FC layers. div.head: V. END-TO-END CAPABILITY AND SCHEDULING CO-DESIGN
div.p: We coordinate the capability selection, heterogeneous resource allocation, and run-time scheduling to optimize control performance by a comprehensive end-to-end capability and scheduling co-design.

div.head: A. Scheduling of Concurrent Intelligent Control Tasks on
div.p: Heterogeneous Platforms 1) End-to-End Response Time Analysis: In this work, tasks are globally scheduled on both CPU and accelerators with fixed-priority scheduling. The priorities ρ i of each intelligent control task τ i will be derived by the optimization problem introduced later in Sec. V-B, prioritizing the tasks that are critical for the overall control performance. Schedulability test methods for task sets on heterogeneous platforms have been explored recently. We enhance the state-of-art methods for multiple CPU and partitioned GPU [50] to analyze the worst-case response time (WCRT) of tasks. The WCRT of task τ i is defined as R ρ i under priority assignment ρ, which is the maximum time interval between the release time and finishing time of τ i . Since a CS could be preempted by higher-priority CSs, while an AS could be blocked but cannot be preempted by other ASs, R ρ i is calculated by summing up the WCRT of CSs R m,ρ i , and the execution time of ASs A m i , and the block time B m i , where m is the segment index in Eq. ( 2). More specifically, considering a taskset τ " tτ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ N u with priority ρ " tρ 1 , ρ 2 , ..., ρ N u, the WCRT of task τ i , i P t1, 2, ..., N u is

div.p: Comparing to Theorem 4.4 in [50], we add the blocking time term since we regard each accelerator as an entity to fully utilize the computation resource instead of partitioning accelerator to execute tasks independently. In such condition, ASs of other tasks may block AS of the current task, i.e., B m i , which is calculated according to Lemma 2 in [43]:

div.p: The blocking time introduced an interesting trade-off that whether putting consecutive layers of DNN on accelerators is worthwhile since long AS may prolong the blocking time to other tasks. However, if consecutive allocation is interrupted, extra memory copy cost is induced. It is nontrivial to find the balance between them.

div.p: 1) Problem Formulation: Based on the modelings of capability, task execution, response time analysis, and utilization in previous sections, the ultimate optimization problem of capability and scheduling co-design is formulated as Prob. (13). minimize li,j ,bi,ρi,iPr1,N s,jPr1,Lis

Different complexity candidates rL bi i , to bi i,j us, b i P t1, 2, ..., Ξu are generated, where Ξ is the number of candidates. Given plant dynamics f i p¨q, environment condition ϵ i , and computation configurations (π i,j , η i,j , and ϕ i,j ), DNN complexity c i is indicated by candidate index b i , and end-to-end response time is R ρ i , which is calculated by c i , tl i,j u, and ρ. Thus, the control performance J i is derived by the control capability function in Eq. (4).

div.p: The optimization objective (13a) is the overall control performance of N control tasks, w i indicates the specified importance of control loop i. Inequation (13b) are the constraints of WCRT of each control task considering the interferences from other tasks, with the deadline of τ i , D i ď T i , as the bound. As introduced in Sec. V-A1, R ρ i depends on priority assignment ρ and resource allocation results l i,j , A m i , and C m i , and DNN complexity c i " rL i , to i,j , j P t0, 1, ..., L i uus. (13c) and (13d) indicate the constraints of CPU and accelerator resource utilization, respectively, where λ C , λ A are EWCET safe margins since the empirical execution time profiling may not cover real worst-case execution time, which can be adjusted based on the fluctuation of the profiled execution time or the stringency of timing performance.

2) Problem Solution-DRL Solver: Since the design space of optimization variables is quite large, the constraints are nonlinear and mixed integer, and the control capability function is derived by data-driven approaches, it is challenging to find the solution of (13). Therefore, we adopt the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework based on Deep Q-Network (DQN) to solve Prob. ( 13), with reward, state and action space designed carefully. The state vector to be optimized is x " rtl i,j u, tb i u, ρs of all tasks. Thus the performance of x is evaluated by J pxq " ř N i"1 J i ptl i,j u, b i , ρq. At each optimization step t, an action a t is selected from the set of legal actions, i.e, for tl i,j u, the legal actions are toggling the variable, and for tb i u and tρ i u, they are trying the value of the previous or next ones in their candidate set. Once action a t is taken, state xt`1 is derived, so as the reward r t that judges a t in the perspective control performance, i.e., r t " J px t q ´J px t`1 q. And if the state xt`1 violates constraints (13b) to (13d), the reward is assigned with a large negative value as a penalty. Correspondingly, if an action makes state xt`1 satisfy constraints that xt does not, the reward is assigned a large positive value. Both values are The action-value function Qp¨q of DQN is constructed by a lightweight NN [51]- [53] to obtain action a t " arg max a Qpx t , aq for state xt . The replay buffer stores state transition tuples px t , a t , r t , xt`1 q, which are used to train Qp¨q. The optimization is processed until the optimized control performance stays for specified episodes without degradation. The optimization time costs depend on the state space. With N " 3, Ξ " 10, maxtL i u " 23, the overheads of solving Prob. ( 13) are 82 minutes on average, which is acceptable since the problem is solved offline. And through reward function adjustment, heuristic methods, and decreasing iteration episodes, the time cost of DRL can be decreased with acceptable performance loss. For instance, we reduce the length of specified episodes without improvement from 500 to 100. For the 3-task case, the time cost is decreased from 82 minutes to 308 seconds with only 9.8% performance loss on average among 40 tests. For 6/9/12-task conditions, the time costs are 1892/3271/6257 seconds among 5 tests without fluctuation. In our future work, we will simplify the problemsolving process and apply capability and scheduling co-design at the run-time.

div.head: VI. CASE STUDY ON AUTONOMOUS QUADCOPTERS
A. AirSim-based Real-time Intelligent Control Simulator
div.p: To evaluate the performance of the intelligent control with capability and scheduling co-design in real-world applications, we developed a hardware-in-the-loop simulator, AirSim-based Real-time Intelligent Control Simulator (ARICS). Note that SCENIC can be applied to any multi-loop intelligent control system that shares the same heterogeneous computation platform, such as execution of multiple parallel functions with limited computation resources on vehicles [54] and multi-node execution in robot operating system (ROS) deployed on single computation station [55]. The case study of quadcopter flight in this section is just a showcase of SCENIC. As shown in Fig. 8, ARICS integrates 1) intelligent control tasks executing on real heterogeneous computing platforms; 2) the AirSim platform [56], which simulates quadcopters in real-time; 3) real Ethernet networks that connect the real heterogeneous computing platform and simulated quadcopters; and 4) the interfaces among the above modules.

AirSim Simulator: AirSim, developed by Microsoft, is an open-source simulation platform designed for developing or testing autonomous vehicles, such as quadcopters and cars in a highly realistic virtual environment. Utilizing Unreal Engine, it provides high-fidelity visuals and physics and supports multiple scenarios. We apply AirSim to simulate multiple real-time dynamics of quadcopters and the environments that the quadcopters experience. Our control goal is to navigate multiple quadcopters to pass through multiple obstructive gates at different positions, as shown in Fig. 9a. By importing customized gate assets, we can create diverse scenarios with gates placed in any position. Since we focus on the intelligent control, we assume the positions of gates (ϵ i ) are known in advance and stored on the heterogeneous platform and the state vector x i pkq " rp i pkq, v i pkq, q i pkqs J of the quadcopter can be collected accurately by the sensors on the quadcopter. Intelligent Controllers on Heterogeneous Platform: We consider the scenario where a single heterogeneous platform controls multiple quadcopters with different gate positions concurrently. This is a typical application of edge intelligent control where the edge (heterogeneous platform) stores the environmental information, such as positions of gates ϵ i , collects the state vectors x i pkq of all quadcopters, and is equipped relatively higher computation resources than the local computation unit of the quadcopter. When sensor data x i pkq " rp i pkq, q i pkq, v i pkqs J arrives at the heterogeneous platform, the state of the nearest gate rp g pkq, r g pkqs is derived according to map information ϵ i and x i pkq. The inputs of intelligent controller are ψ i pkq " rp i,g pkq ´pi pkq, r i,g pkq ŕi pkq, v i pkq, 9
v i pkqs J .

The intelligent controllers g i,ci pψ i pkqq, designed in Section IV-C, are capable of path planning and flight control. The control tasks that execute g i,ci pψ i pkqq are released periodically with the reception of the sensor data x i pkq from the quadcopter in AirSim. The execution patterns of intelligent controllers can be customized and specified according to the controller design and scheduling strategies, including the complexity of DNN, resource allocation, and priorities, which we will discuss in detail in Sec. VI-B. When the calculation is finished, the control commands u i pkq " rF pkq, Ωpkq J s J are sent back to the quadcopter.

Ethernet Networks and Interfaces: Data transmissions between AirSim and the heterogeneous platform are implemented by sockets via the Ethernet network. Regarding the interface programs, each Sensor Client i alongside AirSim simulator repeatedly samples x i pkq from AirSim by API calling with the frequency of T i " 20Hz and forwards it to Sensor Server i via Ethernet. Once x i pkq arrives, the input of intelligent controllers ψ i pkq is generated, and then the intelligent controller tasks are released. Once the computation is finished, the control commands u i pkq are sent to Control Client i and then forwarded to Control Server i, and actuated immediately on quadcopter i by AirSim API call.

div.head: B. Experimental Settings
div.p: 1) System Setups: The AirSim is running on desktop PCs with Intel i5-12490F CPU@3.00 GHz and NVIDIA RTX 3060 GPU@1.78 GHz with high-granularity real-time simulation of multiple quadcopters simultaneously. The heterogeneous computing platform for intelligent control is NVIDIA TX2, where two ARM Cortex-A57 CPUs@2.00 GHz and 256core NVIDIA Pascal GPU@1.30 GHz are used by the intelligent controller. The CPU segments (CSs) of g i,ci p¨q are implemented in C language, while the accelerator segments (ASs) are deployed on GPU by CUDA kernels. For the optimization problem described in Eq. ( 13), γ C and γ A are set to 2 and 1 since we use two of the CPU cores and utilize GPU as an entity. Since we observed the PWCET of GPU fluctuates more, ω c and ω a are set to 1 and 1.1, respectively. For the design space of model complexity c i , two candidate complexity sets are established. Set I involves DNN controllers with depth L i P t3, 5, ..., 23u, and o i,j , 1 ď j ď L i ´1 fixed to 1024. Set II considers both L i and layer sizes o i,j , 1 ď j ď L i ´1, with pL i , o i,j q pairs P tp5, 128q,p7, 128q,p7, 256q,p9, 256q, p9, 512q,p11, 512q, p11,1024q,p13, 1024qu. The weights w i , i P t1, 2, ..., N u, are assigned to 1.

2) Environment Condition and Competition Group Setups: The environmental condition, ϵ i , is defined as the Manhattan distances along y-axis and z-axis between centers of the five gates to be passed through by quadcopter i, i.e.,
div.formula: ϵ i " |p α g,y ´pα`1 g,y | `|p α g,z
div.p: ´pα`1 g,z | with five gate positions p α g , α " 1, 2, ..., 5, representing various levels of difficulties for deploying quadcopter control. Different environmental conditions correspond to varying demands for end-to-end latency. And gate positions on x direction are fixed to p α g,x " 10α m. In the following experiments, three quadcopters modeled in Eq. ( 9) are simultaneously controlled on NVIDIA Jetson TX2. To ensure the concurrent execution of DNN tasks throughout the control process, all quadcopters depart simultaneously. If they reach the center of the fifth gate (target point), quadcopters continue flying until all quadcopters have arrived at their target points.

To assess the control performance of the competition, the starting points are fixed at p i " p0, 10i, 2q and optimal reference paths rx ref,i , u ref,i s are generated offline based on analytical path planning by stringing the starting point and all centers of each gate, assuming perfect and zerolatency controller are applied, i.e., let x i pkq " x ref,i pkq and u i pkq " u ref,i pkq. The control performance is calculated based on Eq. ( 10) with Q x " I 10 , R u " 0.1I 10 . Competition groups are set under different ϵ i . More specifically, we fixed ϵ 2 and ϵ 3 to 1.2 and 2.1, respectively, while changing ϵ 1 P t0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2, 1.5, 1.8, 2.1u with increasing difficulties to pass through all gates. For every ϵ i , the competitions are repeated for 5 rounds (in each boxplot).

3) Approaches: We compare SCENIC to three state-of-theart design approaches, i.e., minimizing overall latency [33], [34] and overall model accuracy [26], [27] of concurrent DNN executions, which are common goals in the perspective of scheduling and intelligent model construction, respectively.

‚ Our proposed capability and scheduling co-design approach (SCENIC) as SC. ‚ Fixed complexities (DC), greedy resource allocation described in Sec. IV-C2, and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling. ‚ Accuracy (AC): The optimization objective is the sum of MSE loss for all DNN controllers, i.e., ř N i"1 β i . ‚ Latency (LA): The optimization objective is the sum of latency for all DNN controllers, i.e., ř N i"1 R ρ i . To ensure the fairness of the comparisons, the other settings of optimizations of SCENIC, AC, and LA stay equal except for the optimization objectives in Prob. (13). ) 1) Optimization results analysis: Under complexity set I, i.e., L i P t3, 5, ..., 23u and o i,j " 1024, 1 ď j ď L i ´1, since AC and LA method do not consider control performance, solutions of LA and AC stay the same with varying ϵ 1 . Fig. 10a shows that for SC the depths L i of three control loops. We can see that L 1 (of loop 1) increases gradually as ϵ 1 increases. L 2 (of loop 2) stays low since latency is more important than DNN model complexity with moderate competition difficulty. L 3 (of loop 3) stays high since DNN model complexity is more important than latency with high competition difficulty. In this case, with only 3 layers for all controllers for LA, there is no layer assigned to GPU for loops 1 and 3 to avoid extra blocking time to loop 2, since the blocking time caused by assigning more layers on GPU is larger than the time saved in computation.

div.head: LA
div.p: Fig. 10b shows AS ratios, i.e., A i {pC i `Ai q, to demonstrate the results of resource allocation, while Fig. 10c shows the priority of each control task in the priority-based scheduling strategy. Since the control performance depends on multiple factors, the variation of AS ratio and priority is not strictly monotonic, which demonstrates the necessity of comprehensive capability and scheduling co-design. When ϵ 1 is relatively small, SC firstly tries to increase ρ 1 to shorten the response time as ϵ 1 increases to 0.9. As ϵ 1 increases to 1.2, AS ratio of loop 1 increases and is equal to that of loop 2. Priority of loop 2 also increases to be equal to that of loop 1 since ϵ 1 " ϵ 2 " 1.2. At ϵ 1 " 1.5, the depth L 1 increases to 11 since low L 1 cannot handle the environmental difficulty, and ρ 1 further increases. As ϵ 1 increases to 1.8, the increase in priority is not enough to address the demand for additional environmental difficulty. Thus, AS ratio of loop 2 is sacrificed and given to loop 1 to shorten the response time of loop 1. At the same time, since improving AS ratio is sufficient to meet the requirements and SC avoids sacrificing the performance of loop 2 too much, ρ 1 decreases. Finally, at ϵ 1 " 2.1, more accelerator resources are assigned to loop 1 to shorten the response time of loop 1.

2) The timing performance: Fig. 11 shows the theoretical WCRT (TR) and actual WCRT (AR). LA gains the shortest latency, while AC gets the longest latency since it pursues complex models with high accuracy. For SC, the changes in WCRTs do not show monotonic trends due to the intertwined relationship between the decision variables. However, we can find that the trends between TRs and ARs are almost consistent. The deadline constraints are met by TRs. All ARs are much shorter than the actual deadline of T i " 50 ms.

3) End-to-end control performance: The end-to-end overall control performances are shown in Fig. 12. We can see that LA performs the worst since simple DNN model cannot handle different competition. The performance of DC varies with different c i , and the optimal c i varies with different ϵ 1 , which demonstrates the rationality tailor model complexities for different control systems. Both AC and SC perform relatively well. SC further improves the control performance by up to 34.52% comparing to AC, since SC is empowered by the control capability function. Then, we look into the overall and per-loop control performance of AC and SC under different ϵ 1 , as shown in Fig. 13. We can see in Fig. 13a that the overall control performance of SC shows significant advantages (from 20.72% to 34.52%) over AC across all ϵ 1 . In more detail, as Fig. 13c shows, to maintain and optimize the overall control performance, the control performance of loop 2 is gradually sacrificed to optimize the control performance of loop 1 as ϵ 1 increases. It is not loop 3 to be sacrificed since loop 3 is more sensitive to delay and complexity due to its competition difficulty. And for AC in Fig. 13b, the control performance of loop 3 is worse due to ignoring control performance.

4) Impacts of complexity candidates: In order to show the generality of candidate c i in SC, we explore another c i set with pL i , o i,j q in tp5,128q, p7,128q, p7,256q,p9,256q, p9,512q,p11,512q,p11,1024q,p13,1024qu. As shown in Fig. 14, the overall control performance with new c i set (SC-tL i , o i,j u) is comparable with the old one (SC-tL i u). The control performance is affected by the granularities of the complexity sets. SC performs better than AC since it considers the control capability and environmental conditions, targeting the overall control performance in an end-to-end architecture.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: Modern control systems are embracing intelligent controllers, such as deep neural networks (DNNs), executed on heterogeneous processors. Designing and executing these tasks on heterogeneous platforms is challenging due to conflicts between throughput and latency, as well as tradeoffs among control performance, algorithm capability, and timing constraints. This paper introduces an end-to-end capability and scheduling co-design approach (SCENIC) to efficiently design and execute these intelligent control tasks. This work starts with a control capability function linking performance, controller complexity, computation, and physical plant properties. Then, an optimization of algorithm capability and resource allocation for both offline and run-time stages is presented. Finally, a case study on drone control using Microsoft AirSim proves that the proposed SCENIC outperforms state-of-the-art design methods.
